20792-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-44:
Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, number 442, opens with a visit to a famed old house. The writers seek not the Royal Society's relics, but the body that now holds its rooms. Such curious, plain pieces fill this June issue of the weekly.

Chambers's Journal brought cheap, wholesome reading to vast numbers each week. Facts, tales, travel, and verse shared its small pages. The Chambers brothers aimed to lift readers without boring them. This one number shows the mix at work: a walk through London rooms turns into a chat on science, memory, and change.
20793-chambers-s-edinburgh-journal-no-44:
Nature never runs out, argues Chambers's Edinburgh Journal, number 443, but our power to enjoy her can fade. Some natures lack that power from the start, the essay says. Whole ages, too, may hold it only in part.

Weekly numbers like this one mixed essays, tales, facts, and verse for family reading. The Chambers firm sold sound reading at a price working folk could pay. Each issue is a small window on what held British minds that week. Number 443's turn toward nature and taste shows the journal's calm, thoughtful tone at its best.
21971-a-son-of-the-sun:
South Seas trading and trickery fill Jack London's A Son of the Sun, a set of tales published in 1912. The title story opens on the schooner Willi-Waw, anchored in a glassy passage between reefs. Her rusty chain wanders over living coral like a monstrous snake while rock-cod play below. On deck, islanders scrape the teak rail under the eye of David Grief, the sun-tanned trader hero of the tales.

Other stories bring the devils of Fuatino, the jokers of New Gibbon, and a little account settled with Swithin Hall. London knew these waters from his own cruising. Grief is his ideal of the white trader: fair, hard, and smarter than the beachcombers and rogues around him. The tales smell of copra, coral, and salt.
23220-the-gray-nun:
Nataly von Eschstruth's The Gray Nun is a tale of mystery built around a veiled figure. White linen bands wrap the woman's head and chin, hiding even her mouth. A black velvet mask covers her brow and upper face, and loose sleeves hide her hands.

What cannot be hidden is her gaze. The blackness of her eyes is so intense that scarcely any whites can be seen. Eschstruth gives readers a figure defined by coverings, where one penetrating stare does all the work. The scene promises secrets, disguises, and a truth kept carefully out of sight.
23262-chasing-the-sun: Chasing the Sun tells of a hero credited with more hand-to-hand fights than the heroes of Greece or Rome ever faced. As a grown man he repeatedly risked his own life to save others, often in plain view of those who had doubted him. Strangest of all, many of his boyhood enemies ended, in time, as his closest friends and allies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anastasius-gr:
Anastasius Grun was the pen name of Anton Alexander, Count von Auersperg, an Austrian poet born at Laibach in 1806 and dead at Graz in 1876. He trained at the Theresian academy in Vienna and studied philosophy and law at Vienna and Graz. From 1831 he managed his family estates at Thurn, travelling in Italy, France, and England before marrying a countess in 1839.

His poems made him famous as a champion of liberalism, and he entered politics, winning election to the National Assembly at Frankfort in 1848. Disappointed there, he withdrew to private life, then returned as a life member of the Austrian Reichsrat. His early lyrics appeared in 1830, followed by a romantic cycle praising Emperor Maximilian I and, in 1831, anonymous political poems that attacked the rule of his day. His complete works were edited in five volumes in 1877.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrew-of-wyn:
Andrew of Wyntoun, Scottish chronicler, was born about the middle of the fourteenth century, in David II's reign. He was perhaps related to Alan of Wyntoun, who married Seton's heiress. He became a canon-regular of Saint Andrews priory, and before 1395 prior of Lochleven, its subject house for centuries.

The Saint Andrews register holds his acts as Lochleven prior from 1395 to 1413, but nothing shows when he died. At Sir John de Wemyss's request, he wrote his Orygynale Cronykil of Scotland, so called because it begins at the beginning of things, with the creation of angels. Since Robert, Duke of Albany, appears as dead, it was finished after September 1420. Writing its latter part, he called himself an old man, so he did not live long after. The manuscripts show revision, by his own hand. No printed edition appeared until 1795, when Macpherson edited it, omitting a third, restored by Laing in 1872.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-attila-the-hu:
Attila, king and general of the Huns until his death in 453, took over disorganized Scythian hordes in 433. He forged them into a feared force across Europe and Asia, invading the Eastern Roman Empire in 441 and then sweeping into Gaul. In 451, allied Romans under Aetius and Visigoths under Theodoric met him on the Plains of Chalons and turned him back.

The next spring he ravaged Aquileia and Lombard cities and marched toward Rome. An embassy near Mantua, led in influence by Pope Leo I, talked him out of sacking the city. For Catholic readers, the entry stresses the bishops of France and Italy who faced him down, above all the pope. It closes with the legends nations later wove around him, best known as Etzel in the Nibelungenlied.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-autun:
Autun, ancient Augustodunum, is a diocese covering the Saone-et-Loire department in France. Under the old regime it answered to Lyons. After the Revolution it joined Chalons and Macon, answering to Besancon in 1802 and to Lyons in 1822. Christian teaching reached Autun early, as the Greek inscription of Pectorius from the third century shows, found in 1839 in the cemetery of St Peter. It witnesses to baptism and to the words of the Eucharist.

Legend sends St Irenaeus's priests Benignus, Andochius, and Thyrsus toward Autun in the sixth-century persecution cycle. Tradition names St Amator, about 250, as bishop, while the first bishop known to history is St Reticius, a writer and contemporary of Constantine. The see won the right to the pallium, the archbishop's woolen band, from Gregory the Great in 599. Later bishops loomed in Merovingian politics, and Autun councils legislated against simony, the buying of church office, and monastic encroachments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernardino-de:
Bernardino de Sahagún, a Franciscan missionary and pioneer student of Aztec culture, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Sahagún in Spain in or before 1500, he died at Mexico in 1590 after more than sixty years in the country. Sent out in 1529, he taught at the college of Santa Cruz in Tlatelolco.

There he preached, converted, and taught native youth Spanish, Latin, science, music, and religion, while mastering Nahuatl, the Aztec tongue, through daily practice. His great manuscript on Aztec life, finished in 1569 with a grammar and dictionary, went unpublished for fear of reviving pagan memory. It survives as a foundation of Mexican ethnology.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-lebru:
An entry on Charles Lebrun, the French historical painter who shaped court art under Louis XIV. Born in Paris in 1619 and trained first by his father, then in the studio of Vouet, he caught the eye of Poussin and spent four years in Italy from 1642. Back in France he won commissions from Fouquet and Queen Anne of Austria, and Cardinal Mazarin introduced him to the king, where he soon held sway over nearly all artistic matters.

Lebrun helped found the Academy in 1648. When Colbert set up the Gobelin tapestry works in 1662, he became its director, designing cartoons, the full-scale drawings for tapestries, and decorations for Versailles, Sceaux, and Marly. After Colbert died in 1683 he lost his patron and withdrew from court into melancholy. The entry admires his energy and colour sense while finding his grand manner heavy and not wholly good for French art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gibail-and-ba: A 1913 entry on Gibail and Batrun — the Maronite eparchies. Siméon Vailhé gives their ancient story. Their bishops guard the Lebanese flock. The cedars guard the mountain towns. The sees of the Phoenician shore. Their 1736 synod is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-honorius-of-a: This 1913 reference article on Honorius of Autun — the twelfth-century scholar. William Turner honors his famous Elucidarium. His pen ordered the learned lore. The schools prized the mighty tome. The encyclopedist of the medieval age. His 1151 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-clopinel: A 1913 entry on Jean de Meun — the Rose's continuer. Pierre Marique honors his famous satire. His pen mocked the courtly love. The age prized the bold verse. The manuscripts keep his name. His 1305 death is famed. His 1280 Rose is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pectorius-of-: This biographical entry profiles Pectorius of Autun, a Christian of Roman Gaul known from his famous inscription, tracing his story and its significance as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's patristic gallery, preserved among the Christians of Gaul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-placidus-brau: This biographical entry profiles Placidus Braun, a German Benedictine historian of the 1800s, tracing his career, his histories, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's monastic gallery, preserved among its Bavarian historians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-of-mel: Robert of Melun was the bishop-theologian of Hereford. This entry notes his Sentences, his episcopate, and his age. The master of the Paris schools: his weighty Sentences taught the clerks of Paris's schools in the 1150s' years of study and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-john-of: St. John of Sahagún was the Augustinian peacemaker. This entry notes his preaching, his miracles, and his cult. The apostle of Salamanca: his fiery word reconciled the factions in Salamanca's streets in the 1400s' decades of Spain's kings in Castile.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-of-au: Stephen of Autun was the bishop of the French see. This entry traces his council, his Cluny, and his fame. The prelate of the Burgundian church: his ancient see crowned Autun in the 1120s' Saône in the river of the Morvan.
doe-osti-17028722-collaborative-r-d-with: First Solar's panel limits got a joint DOE study, and this report hunts the CdTe performance bottlenecks. The pages share the lab findings. The solar makers get their diagnosis. The hunt was joint. The bottlenecks were hunted. The study was joint.
doe-osti-2575366-building-collaboration-: California farm dust met climate science, and this DOE report builds the San Joaquin research team. The pages detail the joint work. The scientists get their playbook. The playbook was dusty. The dust was farm. The team was research. The work was joint.
doe-osti-3018051-computationally-designe: Tiny protein coils that stack themselves got their DOE design doc, and this text folds the bundlemers. The pages detail the assembly results. The materials folks get their data. The doc was computational. The nanoparticles were model. The coils were coiled.
doe-osti-3030029-data-enhanced-resilienc: Neighborhood microgrids getting tougher with data got their DOE planning slides, and this deck maps the resilient operations. The pages detail the results. The grid folks get their deck. The slides were community. The tougher were getting. The slides were community.
doe-osti-3365762-evaluation-for-qflex-be: QFlex got beta-evaluated, and this DOE text covers the beta run. The pages detail the findings. The engineers get their data. The evaluation was beta run. The data were engineer. The QFlex were run. The beta were evaluation. The engineers were data.
doe-osti-3366201-micro2macro-origins-of-: Micro2Macro got climate-origined, and this DOE text covers change uncertainty. The pages detail the findings. The climate folks get their data. The uncertainty was climate change. The data were climate. The Micro2Macro were origins. The change were climate.
doe-osti-3393788-self-leveling-inks-for-: Inks got self-leveled, and this DOE text prints perovskite modules. The pages detail the ultra findings. The energy folks get their data. The flexography was uniform. The data were energy. The modules were solar. The perovskite were printing. The flexography were inks.
doe-osti-3684099-dielectric-spectroscopy: Cables got dielectric-NDE'd, and this DOE text covers unequal aging lengths. The pages detail the spectroscopy findings. The engineers get their data. The NDE was cable. The data were engineer. The lengths were different. The cable were spectroscopy. The unequal were aging.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-in: FBI interviews from June 2002 collected for the 9/11 Commission. The commission pressed deeper into the record. These pages preserve those interviews. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.

FBI interviews from June 2004 collected for the 9/11 Commission. The report's release was weeks away. These pages preserve those final interviews. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.

FBI investigative records from June 2002 gathered for the commission. The public hearings drew nearer. These pages preserve that material. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
fbi-vault-9-11-commission-report-9-11-th: FBI threat notifications from June 2001 for the 9/11 Commission. The intelligence chatter grew louder. This file preserves those warnings. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
flying-for-france-with-the-american-esca:
James R. McConnell's Flying for France tells of the American Escadrille at Verdun, from a sergeant-pilot in the French Flying Corps. McConnell dedicates the book to Mrs. Alice S. Weeks, who lost a son in the French Army and mothered many other Americans in the war.

Chapters cover Verdun, the move to the Somme, McConnell's personal letters, how France trains pilot aviators, and fighting against odds. Photographs show the Americans who flew for France, including Kiffin Rockwell, killed in an air duel over Verdun, and the squadron's lion mascot Whiskey. Readers of First World War aviation will find McConnell's account immediate, modest and moving.
govdocs-archive_org-UAP_Encounters_Relea:
FBI file 62-HQ-83894 is one of the Bureau's central files on unidentified aerial phenomena, and this release covers serials 246 through 301. The excerpts come from the FBI's Central Records Center and were declassified for the UAP Encounters release.

Inside are the Bureau's working papers on sightings, including photographs and correspondence sent in by the public and other agencies. The documents show how reports were logged, checked, and filed over the years, in agents' own wording. For researchers, the value lies in the raw record: what the FBI actually collected, rather than later summaries of it.
in-homespun:
E. Nesbit published In Homespun in London in 1896, a book of short tales told in village voices. Her preface, written from Kent, explains that the stories use the plain speech of South Kent and Sussex country folk. She warns scholars the dialect is living talk, not a puzzle needing a glossary. Each tale is narrated by an ordinary local person.

Stories include The Bristol Bowl, Barring the Way, A Death-Bed Confession, and Her Marriage Lines. Cousins compete for an aunt's savings, sons go guilty or astray, and lovers find one way of love. Nesbit lets her narrators ramble, digress, and judge their neighbours freely. The homespun manner, meaning rough home-made cloth, gives the book its warmth. Village pride, money, and Providence shape every small drama.
narrative-of-the-life-of-moses-grandy-la:
Moses Grandy tells his life as a slave in the United States here. Oliver Johnson issued the book in Boston in 1844. Sales aided his kin who were still held in slavery. A quote from William Pitt fronts the tale.

Pitt calls slavery incurable injustice that must be wiped out whole. The editor notes Grandy could not read or write. Slave laws had kept him illiterate, so names follow his speech. An abolitionist friend's letter brought Grandy to London in 1842. His plain tale of work, family loss, and bought freedom stands among the key slave narratives of its age.
nasa-tm-19650012051-considerations-for-o:
George Hondros is named as author of this 1965 Goddard study, though the scan renders parts of the cover poorly. His subject was the ground system for receiving television from the Apollo spacecraft. Apollo would be at lunar distance, about a quarter million miles away. A television signal fades badly over that distance.

Hondros considers how to set up the ground system for the best result. Antenna size, receiver design, and signal handling all affect the picture. Getting live television from the Moon was a public goal as well as a technical one. This study works on the ground half of that problem.
nasa-tm-19700026493-experimental-develop:
Bobby F. Walls, William C. Mastin, and Peter H. Broussard Jr. of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on April 30, 1970. It reviews a development program for lunar surface navigation gear. Astronauts driving on the Moon would need to know where they were at all times.

The authors examine several proposed schemes for crewed navigation, with notes on uncrewed needs. They favor schemes that could be built soon from proven hardware. The report outlines Marshall's own work in this field. Its main stress falls on a dead reckoning system using gyroscopes, then being designed, built, and tested in-house.
nasa-tm-19710011473-preliminary-evaluati:
Gordon K Watson of the Lewis Research Center issued this early evaluation in March 1971 as NASA TM X-52998. Two fuel specimens had spent twenty five hundred hours in flowing hot lithium. Each specimen was a uranium mononitride cylinder wrapped in tungsten lined T-111, a tantalum alloy. The lithium loop ran at a heat near nineteen hundred degrees Fahrenheit.

By looks, weight, chemistry, and metal structure, the specimens suited flowing lithium well. One problem did appear. Room temperature strength tests broke the cladding in a brittle way, along grain boundaries. Heating the cladding in vacuum for one hour at a higher heat restored its bendable strength.
the-adventures-of-captain-bonneville-u-s:
Washington Irving shaped The Adventures of Captain Bonneville from the captain's own journal, first printed in 1837. Bonneville was a United States Army officer whose trips to the Rocky Mountains and the Columbia River form the book's core.

Irving says he met Bonneville while at work on his account of Astoria, at the table of John Jacob Astor. Astor, the patriarch of the American fur trade, drew keen travelers to his board, and Bonneville stood out among them. Irving paints him as a soldier with a trapper and hunter grafted on. Readers get mountain men, fur brigades, and Native nations of the far West, in Irving's smooth and fond prose.
the-bride-of-the-sun: Gaston Leroux wrote The Bride of the Sun, dated 1912, in a copy put out in 1915 by McBride, Nast and Company. The list of books gives the shape of the tale in four parts. Book I is The Golden Sun Bracelet, Book II is The Living Past, also with four. Book III, The Trail of the Ponchos, has five. Book IV is named The Dictator,. No chapter heads are given inside the books, and no page of the tale is shown.
the-foolish-dictionary-an-exhausting-wor:
Wallace Goldsmith drew and wrote The Foolish Dictionary, printed at Boston in 1904, a comic work of reference on unsure English words. The title page credits the text to Gideon Wurdz, a mock scholar.

Wurdz bears grand fake titles: Master of Pholly, Doctor of Loquacious Lunacy, Fellow of the Royal Gibe Society. The book vows to give the origin, meaning, and right and wrong use of words, confused by a few pictures. In the line of Ambrose Bierce's sharp word lists, it turns dry definitions into jokes on fools, bores, fads, and the high talk of the day.
the-lake-gun:
James Fenimore Cooper's short story comes here with an editor's apparatus. Hugh C. MacDougall transcribed and annotated it. He founded the James Fenimore Cooper Society. His notes explain the tale's history. It is one of Cooper's very few short stories. He wrote it in the last year of his life. A gift volume called The Parthenon carried it in 1850. Cooper earned a hundred dollars for it. A limited book edition followed in 1932. Robert E. Spiller introduced that edition.

MacDougall warns readers what they hold. The tale rests on Seneca Lake folklore. The Wandering Jew and the mysterious lake gun figure in it. A supposed Seneca legend underlies it. In fact it is political satire, he says. Demagogues in general are its target. Senator William Henry Seward is its target in particular. The story opens with the Seneca's two wonders. A tree floats balanced above the water first.
the-land-of-the-changing-sun:
Will N. Harben opens his strange tale with two young men waking in a sinking balloon above the clouds. Harry Johnston, an American, revives first and splashes water on Charles Thorndyke, an English gentleman. Both are weak, bloodless, and unsure where they are.

They recall a professor who fell from the car while clinging to a rope. Johnston tried to pull him up, yet the tilting basket nearly threw all three men out. Grief and guilt hang over the pair as the balloon sinks toward an unknown land below them, in a place neither man can yet name or describe clearly.
the-pony-rider-boys-in-the-ozarks-or-the:
Frank Gee Patchin's The Pony Rider Boys in the Ozarks opens in darkness, with a chapter titled A Mysterious Visitor. Professor Zepplin wakes suddenly in his cot and calls out to the boys, but no answer comes. Something has disturbed him, though he cannot say what. The camp lies in stillness, its fire long dead.

The professor steps outside without dressing and listens for several minutes. Then he tiptoes to the tents. Tad Butler and Walter Perkins sleep soundly in one, Ned Rector and Stacy Brown in the other. They breathe the deep sleep that follows a long day riding the rugged Ozark slopes. Zepplin grunts and blames bad dreams and the pie he ate the night before. He troops back to his tent through the chill air.
the-rover-boys-in-the-mountains-or-a-hun: A Hunt for Fun and Fortune subtitles The Rover Boys in the Mountains, dated 1902. Arthur M. Winfield wrote the volume, and its frontispiece is captioned Dinner on the Way. The pages preserved here are title matter only. They include a list of other Rover Boys books by the same author. No introduction or chapter text appears. The mountain hunt itself cannot be described from what is shown. The companion list names volumes on the river, in camp, on land and sea, on the Great Lakes, and out West.
the-virgin-of-the-sun:
H. Rider Haggard first published The Virgin of the Sun in 1922 and dedicates the tale to James Stanley Little. Thirty-five years earlier the two had discussed the vanished empires of Central America. Haggard offers a story of the marvellous Incas of Peru and of a White God who, legend says, rose from the sea there long before Spanish conquerors came robbing and ruining.

An introductory section then turns to collectors of relics washed up by the sea of time. Great collectors, dealers, and museum agents are set aside. The editor-narrator means the small collectors of modest means who love old things for themselves, one of whom supplied the history printed in the book.
the-white-road-to-verdun: Jessie White Mario's White Road to Verdun was published by T. Fisher Unwin in London in 1916. The title page adds a second imprint line in New York for E. P. Dutton. Only the title page and a contents list are present in this record, so her account does not appear. A dedication to the soldiers of France asks them to stand within the light and come always with their faces toward the sun. Contents head a preface and chapters named Ideas, War Weddings, and Whistling Solder, then an appendix.
young-hunters-of-the-lake-or-out-with-ro:
Captain Ralph Bonehill wrote this boys' adventure about four lads on a lake outing. His preface says the tale stands alone yet forms volume three of the Boy Hunters series. Those books treat field, forest, river, and lake in winter and summer. The contents promise swimming, a Fourth of July party, and a camp on Lake Cameron. A ghost story threads through several chapter titles.

Later chapters bring a lost boy, an old hermit's tale, and a dangerous deer hunt. Enemies from earlier volumes return to trouble the camp. The secret of a mysterious voice closes the tale. Readers get outdoor action mixed with a light mystery.
